work.title: Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon

version.value: Allemande of the Suite in G major in Jacquet de La Guerre’s Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon (Paris, 1707), EJG.06, played with both strains repeated
version.note: The labels, the Internet Archive record, the BnF catalogue and the Oiseau-Lyre discography on medieval.org name only an Allemande and a Gigue; none names a book, suite or key, so the identification rests on comparing the recording with the printed scores. Pitch tracking of the transfer (mains hum removed; tuning 25 cents above A = 440, interquartile range 20–30 cents, the same on both sides of the disc) finds an upbeat B4 at about 2.8 s; a G major chord on bar 1 from about 3.3 s, with the left hand running G–F♯–G–A in semiquavers and then B–G–C–A in quavers; a D major chord (A, D, F♯) at about 37 s with the bass descending D–C–B–A; a spread D major chord opening the second strain at about 83.4 s; and a final G major chord at about 173 s. The first strain takes about 40 s and the second about 44 s, and each is played twice. This agrees with the Allemande of the G major suite in the 1707 book (first edition, printed page 21; Wiberg’s edition, printed page 24): four beats to the bar, an upbeat B, a first strain of eight bars closing on D major, and a second strain of nine bars (10–18) that opens on a D major chord and closes on G major; at about 5 s a bar, eight and nine bars take about 40 s and 44 s. Wiberg’s edition lists La Flamande as the first piece of the D minor suite of the 1707 book, which leaves the G major suite with the only Allemande. None of the four allemandes of the 1687 book is in G major (D minor, G minor, A minor, F major). The F major allemande (EJG.04), the only one that a transfer a whole tone sharp could turn into G major, has an upbeat C and a first strain of seven bars, against the recording’s upbeat B and eight bars; its bar 1 bass line (F–C–F–G–A–B♭) differs from the recording’s even after transposition, and the file sounds a quarter of a semitone sharp on both sides with no whole-tone offset. The earlier proposal of the F major suite could not be reproduced. The Gigue on the reverse comes from the other suite of the 1707 book, in D minor, so the two sides of the disc are from different suites; no source states the pairing.

performers.note: The Bibliothèque nationale de France record reads “Isabelle Nef, clav.” and gives her dates as 1898–1976. The make of the instrument is not established.

date.note: The recording date is not stated in the sources consulted. The BnF record dates the disc 1942; an Oiseau-Lyre discography after Jim Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising (1994) gives its release as 1938 or 1939, recording site and date unknown (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm). The Internet Archive upload date of 25 October 2018 is not a session date.

place.note: No recording venue is established by the sources.

label.note: Named as publisher in the Internet Archive item. The label issued its first 78 rpm discs in December 1937.

catalogue.note: The Internet Archive description gives “Catalog number: O. L. 75”, and the label scan reads “O. L. 75” on both sides.

matrixTakeSides.value: PART 1295 (Allemande); the reverse side, the Gigue, is PART 1296

credits.note: The item’s description names an audio engineer at George Blood, L.P., and lists the item in the Boston Public Library and George Blood collections.

processing.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four stylus sizes, flat and equalised; the engineer’s preferred version is the one offered, as a variable-bitrate MP3 derived from a 24-bit FLAC.
processing.note: The pitch of the file is about 25 cents above A = 440 (interquartile range 20–30 cents), the same on both sides of the disc, and the identified score is in G major, which sounds as written. The offset cannot be divided between the harpsichord’s tuning and the speed of the disc or its transfer; no speed correction was applied here.

digital.format: Internet Archive variable-bitrate MP3 derivative of a 24-bit FLAC transfer of one side of a 78 rpm disc

composition.value: Out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
composition.note: Jacquet de La Guerre died in 1729. This is a term calculation, not clearance of every edition.

recording.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis for a disc dated 1942 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (release in 1938 or 1939 according to an Oiseau-Lyre discography), under the programme’s pre-1963 recording rule.
recording.note: The BnF date is a catalogue date for the disc, not an independently verified first-publication date; an Oiseau-Lyre discography (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm, after Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising) places the release in 1938 or 1939, and the label began issuing discs in December 1937. Either date is before 1963. The Gallica record marks its own digital copy as public domain; the Internet Archive item carries no licence. US first-publication evidence and US status are not established.
